subject: religious-studies
title: The Kalam Argument
welcome_lead: Travel from medieval Baghdad to modern Atlanta, tracing the Kalam argument from al-Ghazali to William Lane Craig.
meta_desc: A-Level Religious Studies adventure on the Kalam cosmological argument.
final_note: A finite past, on Craig's reading, points beyond the universe to a personal cause.

concepts.def: An Islamic theological tradition arguing that the universe has a beginning and therefore a cause; classically defended by al-Ghazali.
Whatever begins to exist has a cause.
Therefore the universe has a cause.
A thought experiment used by Craig to show the absurdity of an actual infinite, supporting a finite past.
Modern scientific evidence that the universe had a beginning approximately 13.8 billion years ago, used by Craig to support premise 2.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Abu Hamid al-Ghazali (1058-1111), in The Incoherence of the Philosophers, argued against the Aristotelian doctrine of an eternal universe, defending creation in time (huduth).

His version of the kalam argument insists that whatever begins to exist has a cause, the world began, and so the world has a cause, namely God.

William Lane Craig's The Kalam Cosmological Argument (1979) defends both premises with philosophical and scientific arguments. Against an actual infinite past, he deploys Hilbert's Hotel and the impossibility of forming an infinite by successive addition.

For premise 2, he appeals to Big Bang cosmology and the Borde-Guth-Vilenkin theorem of 2003 indicating that any expanding universe must have a past boundary.

Craig argues that the cause of the universe must be uncaused, timeless, spaceless, immaterial, immensely powerful, and personal.

It must be personal because only a free agent could selectively bring about a temporal effect from a timeless state without prior conditions to determine it.
